speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If this amendment were to carry, would it prevent the employment of cooperative marketing agencies like the wheat pools?
Yes, I am advised that it would.

Since the wheat board is the sole receiving agency and exporter, is there any reason why it should not have its own selling agency? There seems to be a contradiction there. The wheat board is going to handle all wheat that we are going to sell; we have signed long-term contracts with importing countries and then, after having fixed up these agreements, someone else is to handle the mechanics of placing it for us. This clause permits the government to go into the actual selling, and I understand that this is the first time the government has written this particular clause into the wheat board1 act.
We have always had it.
If it is there, why do we not use it?
The Canadian wheat board is not asking the buyers to use any particular services. They are quite satisfied to carry on the way they have been and use certain established services.
Judging from the answer the minister gave me I would assume that on the wheat taken by Great Britain they pay brokerage charges.
They pay a service charge.
How much does that amount to?
For the movement of wheat from the lakehead to the seaboard, one cent a bushel; for the movement of wheat from Vancouver, half a cent a bushel.

From evidence given by the officials, I have understood that in the past it was the desire of the British government to trade through these brokerage people. Is that the case today? It was during the war.
So far, they have indicated plainly that they wish to continue to trade through the established agencies.

I do not think the minister's conclusion is accurate when he says that the amendment, if carried, would prevent the British from utilizing the pools. It merely
says:
-to establish such marketing agencies or facilities as it deems necessary for the purpose of its operations under this act.
It does not say that before it establishes all that is required for the board's own business, it shall not use the pools.

If it would permit the use of one agency the amendment would mean that the board could establish any channel it liked. If we accept the hon. member's interpretation of the amendment it is just words that mean nothing at all.

I am indebted to the hon. member for Rosthern for pointing out that the amendment might prohibit the pools from selling, which is something I would not wish to do. What I wished to accomplish was this. I should like to see the government do the thing which the bill says it may do. I understand that this is permissive but not obligatory? Is that correct?
That is correct.
In moving the deletion of those words, I was simply proposing to make it obligatory for the board to establish a selling agency of their own.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member not realize that to make it obligatory on the board to set up their own organization might prevent them from employing the cooperative marketing agencies, which have their elevators and terminals and so on out west? If it is made obligatory on the board to set up their own organization it would be impossible for them to employ the pools. Surely the C.C.F. do not want to put the pools out of business.

In answer to the hon. member, I would point out that in the handling of coarse grains, for instance, it did not follow that we had only one marketing agency. The wheat board is taking delivery of coarse grains and the grain trade is also handling coarse grains. The thing I hoped to do by my amendment was to make it obligatory for the board to start to do this thing which this clause says it may do.

I think there is a misunderstanding between the hon. member for Rosthern and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. We want to know what is meant by a marketing agency. The hon. member for Rosthern I think includes all the elevators and he may be right, but I understand that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle means only the commission agents who do the actual buying or selling of the grain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It says, "employ such marketing agencies or facilities."

I agree with the hon. member for Rosthern.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
In view of the explanation given, does the hon. member wish to withdraw her amendment?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I withdraw it.
Amendment withdrawn.

The minister has indicated in answer to questions, that there is now no commission paid by the government or the wheat board and no commission paid by the purchaser, but that what he calls a service charge is paid. Is that correct?
That is what I have stated, yes. The purchaser pays a service charge or commission, or whatever you want to call it, but that is entirely outside the purview of the wheat board.

The minister has indicated that a service charge is paid by the purchaser, of one cent a bushel in some cases and half a cent a bushel in others. What I want to know is what service is given for this charge that is made.
I think I can get an answer for the hon. member, but I do not see that it is relevant at all, because it is a matter between the purchaser and the agent in Canada that he employs.

If the minister does not wish to answer, that is one thing, but I respectfully suggest that the members of this house and the Canadian people ought to be told what service is given for this charge of one cent or half a cent a bushel which the minister has mentioned. I think it would clear up a great deal of misunderstanding if there were more frankness on the part of the minister on that point.

I think this point
should be cleared up. I well remember that in the agriculture committee in 1942, when the report of the wheat board was before that committee, another member and I moved for the names and a break-down of some ninety brokers who were then being paid by the wheat board on the say-so of the other end of the deal. I understand that this practice has been stopped and that the other end of the deal are now paying it themselves, that it does not go through wheat board channels at all. But in 1942 the cheques were issued by the wheat board on the say-so of the purchaser at the other end of the deal.
I have a copy of the proceedings of that committee to bear me out. The commissions ran into a huge sum of money. I think the 
producers are entitled to know just what service is rendered for the service charge that is made, even if it is paid by the other end of the deal, because it is part of the buying and selling operations.

Wheat going from the lakehead to the seaboard is taken by the shipper and put on board the ocean-going vessel. Exactly the same thing takes place with respect to Vancouver; the shipper takes the grain and places it on board an ocean-going vessel.
Is that the same service for which a commission was formerly paid?
Yes.
Then the service charge is just a substitution for the commission which was formerly paid?
Technically it may be a substitution, but actually it is an arrangement between the purchaser and his agent in Winnipeg.

If I may be permitted, what the hon. member for Souris has in mind is, I think, a discussion that took place before the committee on agriculture in 1942. I recall that on that occasion I was called before the committee to answer some questions having to do with the very point which is now raised. This request was made of the British at that time, whether they wanted this service established in Canada. Mr. Taggart was with me in Britain in 1940. The then chairman of the cereals branch of the purchasing board of the British government was Mr. Rank; his assistant was Mr. Hooker. Across the table we asked the definite question whether they wanted this service continued in Canada. They made the definite request at that time that the service be continued on this side; that otherwise they would have to set up a service of their own. They preferred to deal with the individuals who had been carrying on the service throughout the years and with whom they were familiar rather than to establish one of their own. They have been dealing in that way ever since. The officials on the British side who are dealing with the wheat at the present time are much the same officials who were dealing with it then.

Paragraph (e) of subsection 3 of section 2 confers certain powers upon the board. It gives the board power-
. . . to employ such technical, professional or other officers, clerks or employees as may be lecessary for the conduct of its business.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I presume that power was conferred upon the board by order in council under the War Measures Act, but I am not sure of this. However I think the wisdom of conferring such power upon the board is open to question. In a great many lines of governmental activity civil servants are chosen by the civil service commission. Personally I am opposed to conferring this power upon the board, because I think the civil service commission might very well be employed to choose these officials. Of course it might be said that the civil service commission are not capable of employing or choosing technical and professional officers. I should like to point out that the Gordon report made certain recommendations about modifying the position about technical and professional officers under the Civil Service Act. Personally and, I think, on behalf of the party I can say that we are not opposed to such a change, but if the government keeps on appointing officials m this way the day will come, and it may not be far distant, when there will be more civil servants outside the provisions of the Civil Service Act than there will be under it. Therefore I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Souris:
That section 2 be amended by deleting from the first line of paragraph (e) of subsection 3 thereof the words, "notwithstanding anything contained in," and substituting therefor the words, "pursuant to the provisions of."
The paragraph would then read:
Pursuant to the provisions of the Civil Service Act, to employ such technical, professional or other officers, clerks or employees as may be necessary for the conduct of its business.
We shall have to give consideration to the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Haldimand, but I may say that this paragraph is taken from the wheat board act of 1935.
No.
You are not following all the features of that act.

I misstated my
information.
It is not in the 1935 act.
The powers are exactly the same as those contained in the act of 1935.

May I ask the minister a question in connection with the main part of the section which provides:
The board is, for all purposes, an agent of His Majesty in right of Canada . . .
Will the minister not reconsider that and perhaps make an addition to the act permit-83166-53
ting the board to be sued? Will he tell me now, if he can, why he thinks this board ought not to 'be sued the same as any other corporation doing business of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps that is a question on Which I might be allowed to say a word or two. I am not in a position at the moment to make a full statement on the desirability or advisability of making boards such as this agencies of the crown. But in the only litigation in which the point has been raised, this board has been held to be an agent of the crown. One thing which I think one can say with certainty is that it is desirable in t'he legislation to settle the question one way or the other as to whether it is an agency of the crown or not. According to other provisions of the act, the board is subject to directions from the governor in council. That may or may not be desirable. The desirability of making it subject to the directions of the governor in council may be dealt with under a subsequent section. But I think parliament will expect t'he government to take a considerable measure of responsibility for the operations of the wheat board, because it is in its essence a government operation.
As I understand it, When it is made an agency of the crown its property is not taxable. I think that is desirable. I should think it would be desirable from the point of view of the farmers who are interested in keeping the expenses of the board as low as possible.
I am not suggesting any change in that. I think you should merely addi a provision somewhere that it can sue and be sued.
Then t'he question of garnishee arises. If this board, is not an agency of the crown I am informed it would probably be subject to garnishee proceedings.
Suppose it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would mean that these amounts due to hundreds of thousands of farmers would be attachable at the instance of creditors. That has never been considered as a desirable feature of the legislation, I do not think it is desirable, although that again is something as to which there might be pros and cons.
A garnishee would cover only debt, not damages or things of that kind.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not mistaken, am I, in thinking that if an amount is due by the crown to a farmer under a participation cer-

Canadian Wheat Board Act

tificate, if that debt could be attached in garnishee proceedings the farmer would not get it. If it is like an independent corporation that would be the situation.
That could be protected, if you want to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Should we attempt to draw a line? As I say, I did not come prepared1 to argue this question and I should like to give it a little further thought. But should we be prepared to set up something halfway between a crown corporation and an independent corporation?
It was done in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether the
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is an agency of the crown or not.
Nobody else does.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is why it should be settled one way or the other in this bill. I think it should be settled one way or the other as to whether it is an independent board entirely, and the more independent it is made, the more you take it from under the control of government and of parliament. Or it should be made an emanation of the crown in so many words, which would bring it directly under the governor in council and much more susceptible, I should saj', to the control of parliament and exemption from taxation and garnishee proceedings. These are some of the considerations involved in deciding the question, and I shall give the matter some thought between now and tomorrow and make a statement as to what our position is. But with what consideration we have been able to give it, we thought it was far more desirable, from every point of view, to make it. an agency of the crown, which in fact it is. Really this is the government, through an agency, that is in the business.

The minister will remember that the most I asked was that he give the matter further consideration than it has so far received.
May I point out one or two other things that have not been considered. Let us assume that this organization, which will be a large one, is driving a motor car down the street and runs over someone. As the section stands, the person injured has no recourse whatever, because you cannot sue the king. I confess that, with respect to the army and the air force during the war, the government was very fair about such matters and permission

was readily given if one had difficulties of the kind I have mentioned. The point I am trying to make, however, is this. I appreciate the difficulties suggested by the Minister of Justice, in taking half measures, so to speak, because when we do that we do not know how many complications we shall run into around the corner. But it seems to me that, if we simply put a clause in there that this is a corporation-we have already got that-[DOT] which may sue and be sued, that would let us out of most of our difficulties and certainly give individuals all their rights.
As to the worry about garnishee proceedings, I do not think that is serious. You cannot garnishee anyone for damages but only for debt, and it is only when the debt is due; that is all. If an individual farmer garnisheed the board for a debt, let us say, of $1,000 it would not hurt the board to pay the $1,000 into court. That is all you do, and I fail to see any great worry about giving the right of garnishment to a person who thinks the board owes him some money.
As regards saying that he has a participation certificate, that can be easily fixed by declaring that that certificate is not payable until a given date and only on that date does it become a debt in connection with which garnishee proceedings can be taken. The difficulties are not so great and I wish the minister would give the matter sympathetic consideration overnight and let us have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The. act now provides that the board may sue and be sued.
I could not find it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is on page 3, section 2 of the bill. Section 2 is an amending section which leaves extant, untouched, subsection 1 of the old section 4 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and subsection 1 reads:
The board shall be a body corporate having capacity to contract and to sue and be sued in the name of the board.
So that the power to sue and the liability to be sued are there. It has, however, been held that this is an agency of the crown, in the only litigation on the point that has come up, and therefore the words which provide that it may sue and be sued mean sue and be sued in the exchequer court and not in the ordinary courts of the province, which does necessitate the obtaining of a fiat. I think I should take some slight exception to a statement made once or twice that a person is without remedy when a fiat is necessary. Fiats are granted universally, though there have been cases

Homing
where obviously a frivolous application has been made and denied. But access to the exchequer court is access to a court of justice in every sense of the word.

Is not the difference between having a fiat and not having one simply that the litigant in one case is at the mercy of the court and in the other at the mercy of the government? If the government does not want to grant the fiat it need not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is theoretical only.
It is more than theoretical. If it is only theoretical, why is there a fiat?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has always been so. When you are suing the crown your first act is to apply for a fiat.
